memory_leads.lead: Containerization was moving from an innovation phase toward dominant long-haul liner practice on major developed-market trades, with ports, rail links, crane systems and inland distribution reorganizing around standardized boxes.

Major ports increasingly faced a strategic split between legacy breakbulk facilities and deep-water container terminals requiring large cranes, marshalling yards and road/rail connectivity; some traditional urban waterfronts likely lost traffic to purpose-built terminals.

memory_leads.lead: The first oil shock likely created extreme tanker-market dislocation: earlier expectations for continued oil-trade growth collided with demand weakness, changed trade flows and a large tanker/orderbook overhang.
VLCC/ULCC scale had expanded rapidly before the oil shock; afterward, tanker lay-ups, slow steaming, conversions and scrapping became important responses to surplus capacity.
Bulk shipping remained tied to iron ore, coal and grain flows, with vessel-size economics increasingly favoring specialized bulk carriers and larger ore/coal routes where port drafts allowed.
unknowns: Capesize terminology and fleet segmentation timing

memory_leads.lead: Early LNG shipping expanded from pioneering 1960s projects into a small but strategically important specialized fleet linked to long-term liquefaction/offtake projects rather than spot commodity trading.
unknowns: How participants viewed LNG shipping risk

memory_leads.lead: Japan was a dominant commercial shipbuilding center, while European yards were under mounting competitive pressure and South Korea was beginning its emergence as a major low-cost large-vessel builder.

memory_leads.lead: MARPOL 73/78 emerged from pollution concerns, especially tanker accidents and oil pollution, creating the foundation for progressively tighter international marine environmental rules.
unknowns: Which technical provisions mattered first to owners

memory_leads.lead: Diesel propulsion, larger hulls, standardized container handling and specialized vessel designs continued replacing older mixed cargo practices; fuel-cost sensitivity rose sharply after oil-price shocks.
unknowns: Fuel-saving operational responses at the time

memory_leads.lead: The post-boom tanker collapse likely left banks, shipowners and shipyards with distressed assets and reinforced shipping's pattern of long order lags followed by severe oversupply.
The Iranian Revolution and second oil shock changed oil prices and trade patterns again, likely tightening some tanker routes even while structural fleet oversupply persisted.

judgment_leads.judgment: Owners/builders may have extrapolated rapid oil-demand and long-haul crude growth into continued need for ever-larger tankers.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Do not use the later tanker depression to rewrite pre-shock optimism.

judgment_leads.judgment: Market participants likely debated whether the tanker slump was cyclical or a durable break caused by energy conservation, changed oil sourcing and massive fleet overhang.
Containerization may have been increasingly viewed as irreversible on major liner trades, but the winning carrier/port structures were still unsettled.
judgment_leads.outcome_boundary: Do not project later global carrier concentration backward.
